openalex_display_name: Feminine images and shadow projection of deracinement in Heart of Darkness
openalex_abstract: In Joseph Conrad's works of depicting sea journey and European colonization,female characters are comparatively fewer and weaker.Yet in his masterpiece Heart of Darkness,there are not only five female characters but also abundant feminine images,from darkness and heart in the title to river,Africa,primitive,land,shadow,etc.which prevail through the whole novel. Do these feminine images have something to do with the sense of guilt of his so-called betrayal to his motherland or are they the shadow projection of his deracinement? The present paper sets to get these feminine images connected with Conrad's miserable childhood,his betrayal to his motherland,his sense of guilt and his deracinement,therefore to interpret how Conrad made use of these feminine images to memorize his childhood and how he gained Katharsis and expiation by means of shadow projection.

openalex_display_name: Combating Injustice: The Naturalism of Frank Norris, Jack London, and John Steinbeck
openalex_abstract: Jon Falsarella Dawson begins Combating Injustice: The Naturalism of Frank Norris, Jack London, and John Steinbeck by proposing a reinterpretation of the familiar literary movement, naturalism, through a distinct theoretical lens, social critique. He is particularly interested in investigating financial and economic questions, a line of inquiry that has not been as frequently applied to naturalist texts. Traditionally, the movement has been linked to its origins in nineteenth-century biological and sociological discourses, particularly the Lamarckian and Spenserian strands that occupied the social imaginary. Such traditional criticism often connected these discourses with recurrent themes of determinism. Dawson pivots within this critical trend, offering an alternative approach to similar thematic concerns. He writes that “economic determinism is central to social criticism in American naturalism” (5). For Dawson, themes of determinism can be closely connected to causative economic forces. Thus, the restriction of the individual’s agency is less biological (as in traditional readings) than economic and social. Dawson proposes that naturalist writers use this economic determinism in service of their broader social critique.Combating Injustice comprises eight chapters. In addition to the book’s introduction and conclusion, each of selected important writers receive two chapters dedicated to their work. Dawson focuses on Norris’s McTeague and The Octopus; London’s Martin Eden, The Iron Heel, and two short stories; and Steinbeck’s In Dubious Battle and The Grapes of Wrath. Each chapter maintains, for the most part, a consistent pattern. Dawson begins by providing historical context for each work, drawing attention to the prevailing political and economic structures. His selection of historical material is acute and directly serves his literary analysis throughout. He then moves to an extended close reading, tracing the texts’ engagement with and transformation of the historical moment. His theoretical approach is brought alongside the text, rather than being callously imposed upon it. Dawson draws numerous compelling examples and repeatedly clarifies how economic forces manifest in these texts. The style of his prose is both measured and clear, articulating nuanced interpretations in an accessible way. In many regards, Dawson’s prose is exemplary, avoiding the opaque jargon that can sometimes detract from literary arguments.His chapters on Norris are especially strong. Dawson emphasizes the cultural weight that issues of monopoly, speculation, and financial innovation carried during Norris’s career and in the fictional world of his novels. In his discussion of both McTeague and The Octopus, Dawson traces how national economic structures circumscribe characters’ actions. Furthermore, he highlights themes of industrial extraction and the “tragedies that emerge from privileging financial gain over the common good” (68). In his treatment of Norris, Dawson emphasizes the power and scope of economic systems. This macro-level concern responds to the ambitious scope of Norris’s wheat trilogy. Norris was interested in the broad mechanics of economy and planned to trace the movements of a single commodity (wheat) from Californian farmers (The Octopus), to Chicagoan distributors (The Pit), and then to European consumers (The Wolf [unwritten]). Dawson’s critique ambitiously engages the mechanics of such large systems.The chapters on London are equally insightful. Dawson shifts from Norris’s emphasis on systems to London’s interest in the cultural repercussions of such structures. Given London’s ardent socialist bent, Dawson’s analysis finds ample instances of political and economic representation. Furthermore, he follows London in paying particular attention to the working conditions that plagued the lower class. Dawson outlines the interpersonal deterioration and individual alienation manifested in London’s proverbial “work-beast” and Martin Eden’s class ascension. He articulates the dehumanizing effects of industrial efficiency. The brutal commitment to mere production transformed a character like Johnny (“The Apostate”) into an “abnormal creature that violates the patterns of the world” (78).Dawson’s chapters on Steinbeck offer excellent introductions to the historical context that deeply informed In Dubious Battle and The Grapes of Wrath. Furthermore, Dawson does a nice job situating Steinbeck’s political perspectives alongside his complex concerns as a writer. For example, in his discussion of In Dubious Battle, Dawson engages Steinbeck’s commentary on the novel: “I have used a small strike in an orchard valley as the symbol of man’s eternal, bitter warfare with himself. . . . I’m not interested in strike as a means of raising wages, and I’m not interested in ranting about justice” (145). On the face of it, this insight weakens an economic and social interpretation of the text. However, Dawson provides a crucial gloss: “While Steinbeck deemphasizes the concrete aims of labor struggles, they do provide the context for the representation of issues fundamental to the human enterprise, an approach that expands the project from a mere muckraking book to an exploration of the forces that animate behavior” (145). Dawson aptly describes how the symbolic approach does not negate the importance of the context. The material conditions of the labor struggle mediate “issues fundamental to the human enterprise.” While In Dubious Battle is not a proletarian novel (the strikers are not idealized), Dawson argues that Steinbeck was not politically neutral. Steinbeck often occupied a liminal space between political poles; on the right, he was too sympathetic to communism; on the left, he was not sympathetic enough. While acknowledging that the text resists the didactic melodrama of a muckraking novel, Dawson argues that Steinbeck clearly emphasizes the need to alter the economic conditions that were responsible for the conflict. Dawson writes, “In Dubious Battle suggests the clash must inevitably take place despite the vast obstacles against the victory of labor in order to alter socioeconomic conditions” (161).In his reading of In Dubious Battle, Dawson also extends his argument regarding economic determinism. He writes that Steinbeck’s animal imagery “reiterates the causative function of the landowners, signifying that the laborers have been reduced to their present conditions by the practices of the powerful” (155). While Dawson acknowledges Steinbeck’s interest in the phalanx, he ultimately places far more emphasis on the causative forces of the owners. Therefore, the strikers’ violent actions are more determined by particular social pressures than the universal phalanx phenomenon. The degree to which Dawson interprets economic determinism in In Dubious Battle may strike some Steinbeck scholars as overstated.In his chapter on The Grapes of Wrath, Dawson continues to extend previous interpretations. He contends that “socioeconomic” forces explain the Joads’ exodus and delineate their actions throughout the novel (162). The deterministic reading is particularly bold throughout this chapter: “representations of capital comprise the primary deterministic agents in The Grapes of Wrath” (167). While such a claim can be closely substantiated by examples from Norris and London (and, to a lesser degree, In Dubious Battle), this economic interpretation may strike some readers as more tenuous in regard to Grapes. The ecological disaster, which Dawson briefly mentions, is explained as an outworking of “economic motives” (169). Considering the cultural, religious, environmental, and political influences that created the Dust Bowl, the attribution of the event to a causative economic base seems reductive. In other places, the theoretical framework feels likewise strained. At one point, Dawson describes Ma Joad’s compassion as “indicating that the poor have an obligation to their class” (184). This “class” language subtly undermines the broader universal compassion that Steinbeck deeply engrains in the novel.Despite these quibbles, Dawson’s broader framework is still a helpful hermeneutic for Grapes, specifically his attention to alienation. In resonance with London’s emphasis on dehumanization, Steinbeck emphasizes the negative effects that accompany instrumental practices and industrial efficiency. Dawson quotes, for instance, this famous descriptive phrase from Grapes: “the machine man, driving a dead tractor on land he does not know or love” (qtd. 168). When the world is approached as a mere accumulation of resources, humanity’s relationship with the natural world becomes sterile. Throughout the book, Dawson repeatedly connects this alienation to broader economic structures. In this sense, his interpretation provides a language to identify such threads of personal and social regression.Dawson concludes Combating Injustice by reiterating that Norris, London, and Steinbeck engage ideas of economic determinism in order to illuminate social issues and ameliorate material conditions (186). The later part of his argument represents a substantial shift in understanding the naturalist mode. Dawson diverts attention from the failings of the individual, writhing under natural and obscure forces, toward the importance of collective action and the potential for improvement. In this way, Dawson provides an optimistic avenue for approaching naturalism; while humanity is restricted by external forces, these forces are largely manufactured and impermanent. Dawson draws our attention to the possibility of reform and revolution, which is manifested across these writers’ work. Combating Injustice is an excellent thematic survey of its selected writers and provides a rich historical overview of American economic tensions, tensions which have remained relevant and important in modern discourse.

openalex_display_name: Ama Ata Aidoo's Heart of Darkness
openalex_abstract: This essay reads Aidoo's novel Our Sister Killjoy as a postcolonial revision of Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness. While both novels have been accused of being racist texts, this essay argues that the implied existence of Conrad's text is crucial for our understanding of Aidoo's racist representational strategies. The drama of Aidoo's novel lies in approaching and refraining from the horror of the racism of Conrad's Heart of Darkness.

openalex_display_name: Coleridgean Contributions
openalex_abstract: By 1802, Coleridge had begun to suspect what the next thirty years would confirm – that there was a ‘radical Difference’ between Wordsworth’s conception of poetry and his own ( CL STC II. 830). Lyrical Ballads was the outcome of a period of initial excitement when, at the start of a relationship, each man was able to suspend his difference and, for a while, be a version of himself that met the other’s hopes and ideals. As such, it was a typical project for Coleridge, who had an intense need to be part of a literary circle in which friendship gave rise to, and was in turn intensified by, communal writing, reading and publishing. He had been co-writing or co-publishing poems with Southey since 1794; in 1797 his first verse collection included poems by his friends Charles Lloyd and Charles Lamb. Wordsworth, on the other hand, had never published collaboratively before and never would again. In a sense, then, Lyrical Ballads (1798) was a Coleridgean volume, one of many co-authored outlets for a practice of versifying that he shared with friends – a practice that was often self-reflexive: the poems were often about the shared experiences of the friends with whom they were written and/or to whom they were recited. A case in point was ‘This Lime Tree Bower My Prison’, the poem in which Coleridge first invoked William and Dorothy in the conversational voice that he and Wordsworth would develop during the next five years. The poem features Charles Lamb as well as the Wordsworths and was recited to them on the spot where it was composed. It was not, however, published in Lyrical Ballads but in Southey’s Annual Anthology alongside contributions by other members of the circle – including Joseph Cottle, the Bristol bookseller who published both it and Lyrical Ballads . This pattern suggests that Lyrical Ballads was just one of many joint publications by which Coleridge sought to promote the innovatory poetic style of the West Country circle, and in so doing endorse their group language. Other poems went into the columns of The Morning Post , where verse by Southey and by Mary Robinson (a satellite member of the group) also appeared.

„Przebudzenie” Kate Chopin, czyli „amerykańska Bovary”(?)
openalex_abstract: This article deals with the question of the so-called Bovarism in The Awakening, the famous novel written by Kate Chopin. When it was first published in 1899, it was universally condemned for its alleged obscenity, just like its French predecessor. It is true, however, that unlike Flaubert’s book, The Awakening did not find itself in the dock, faced with charges of immorality, but the hostile reviews condemned the novel to many decades of obscurity. In this article, I try to return to the question of parallels between the two novels, which can be seen on many levels. Some similarities concern both male and female characters, while others are to do with specific narrative decisions and solutions. The most conspicuous example of the latter is the suicidal death of both heroines.

openalex_display_name: Queer Privilege: Telepathy and Sadomasochism in the Nineteenth Century Novel
openalex_abstract: In nineteenth century novels, depictions of mind-to-mind communication or telepathy are often structured in terms of dominance and submission. This recurring interpersonal and intersubjective dynamic is magnified and typified in Jane Eyre by Charlotte Bronte, Wuthering Heights by Emily Bronte, and The Lifted Veil by George Eliot where telepathy and sadomasochism are depicted as co-constitutive. In these novels, this conceptual dyad, what Queer Privilege refers to as “telepathic sadomasochism”, registers a non-normative or queer subjectivity predicated on the notion that erotic investment in the other alters and empowers the self in ways that transgress categories of identity like gender, class, and sexuality. In Jane Eyre, Wuthering Heights, and The Lifted Veil, this non-normative register of thought, erotics, and being is characterized as a superiority of power and access; in Henry James’ terms, telepathic sadomasochism is a “queer privilege”. Therefore, telepathic sadomasochism is positioned as a sense of empowerment in and through marginalization, a kind of ideal that supersedes the normative. Queer Privilege exploits telepathic sadomasochism as an intertextual site wherein three key Victorian authors hold a discussion regarding the ethics of a sexuality and subjectivity predicated on the eroticization of power and the queering of the self.

Walt Whitman's Split Poetic Personalities
openalex_abstract: Walt Whitman fills his poetry with contradictions and inconsistencies as he explores different solutions to complex spiritual, social, and psychological problems. Such contradictions often take the form of competing first-person characters, each with a different set of beliefs, powers, and experiences. In the 1855 first edition of Leaves of Grass especially, there is a chaotic tension between other and self, unity and difference, transcendence and isolation, knowledge and confusion, reality and façade, and power and weakness. These tensions play out in the realm of the “I” as the narrator regularly shifts his form and his relationship to the world around him.\nTwentieth-century critics have read Whitman from a variety of angles. Most readings identify a division of competing projects or voices, but the nature of the division depends on the particular critical lens at work. In particular, this essay examines D. H. Lawrence, Malcolm Cowley, Harold Bloom, and Vivian Pollak as readers of Whitman. Each of them finds it necessary to reduce the complexity of the poetry, but each also contributes an important critical analysis that expands the discussion of Whitman’s critical tensions and their purposes. Ultimately, I argue that Whitman’s division of contradictory first person voices offers his poetry a unique rhetorical force.
